manifest.author: LTM Cost IQ Methodology
manifest.questionDesign: Full 105-question CIO answer-experience redesign — CORE-01 to CORE-45 reviewed through v6.5; ADP-01 to ADP-20 reviewed in v6.6.
questionDesignPrinciples: CIO hypothesis is captured separately from engine findings and is not treated as evidence.
Initial assessment is hybrid: executive ranges/qualitative responses first; actuals and evidence are validated later.
Cost IQ and Value IQ are executive headline scores with confidence shown independently.
Economic opportunity and practical/actionable opportunity are distinct outputs.
Illustrative savings ranges require evidence validation before any savings commitment.
Stable IDs connect answer -> signal -> score -> finding -> opportunity -> recommendation -> LTM service.
Opportunity sizing distinguishes economic addressability from practical actionability using explicit feasibility constraints.
Trade-off, hypothesis, hotspot and context questions are used as signals and are not scored by option count or position.
Maturity scoring uses semantic option IDs rather than positional A/B/C mappings wherever a deterministic score is intended.

questions.prompt: Which areas of the technology estate account for a material share of technology cost today?
questions.intent: Establish the cost-relevant technology footprint so the assessment only activates diagnostics that are relevant to the enterprise.
questions.answerDesign: Select every area that materially contributes to technology cost. Do not select areas that are immaterial or purely incidental.
questions.evidenceImplication: Sets evidence scope

options.label: On-premises infrastructure and data centres
Private cloud / hosted private infrastructure
Public cloud services
SaaS applications and subscriptions
Enterprise software and licensing
Network and connectivity
Data platforms, storage and analytics
Cybersecurity technology and security platforms
Internal technology workforce
External technology services / managed services
End-user computing and workplace technology
Other material technology spend

questions.answerGuidance: Think beyond the centrally managed IT estate where business-managed technology is material.

questions.prompt: Which industry most closely reflects the organization’s primary business model?
questions.intent: Select the industry context used to tailor later diagnostic questions and interpretation.
questions.answerDesign: Choose one primary industry; select the closest match where the organization spans multiple sectors.
questions.evidenceImplication: Determines relevant evidence areas

options.label: Banking / Financial Services
Insurance
Healthcare / Life Sciences
Manufacturing
Retail / Consumer
Energy / Utilities
Telecommunications
Technology
Travel / Transportation
Public Sector
Professional Services
Other

questions.answerGuidance: Choose the industry that best describes the organization’s principal revenue-generating business.

questions.prompt: What is the organization’s approximate annual revenue?
questions.intent: Establish enterprise scale for interpreting technology economics and normalizing cost without requiring an exact financial figure.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the closest annual revenue band. Use the USD-equivalent band if the enterprise reports in another currency.
questions.evidenceImplication: Improves normalization

options.label: Below US$100M
US$500M–1B
US$1B–5B
US$5B–25B
Above US$25B
Not known / prefer not to disclose

questions.answerGuidance: A broad, recent estimate is sufficient; exact revenue is not required.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate annual technology spend currently in scope for this assessment?
questions.intent: Establish the financial baseline against which cost, value and opportunity signals will later be interpreted.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the closest spend band. Include material technology spend in scope even where it sits outside the central IT budget.
questions.evidenceImplication: Primary financial evidence input

options.label: Below US$5M
US$5M–25M
US$25M–50M
US$500M–1B
Above US$1B
Not known / prefer not to disclose

questions.answerGuidance: Use the figure leadership would consider the most representative current technology-spend baseline.

questions.prompt: Which categories are included in the technology-spend figure you just provided?
questions.intent: Test whether the financial baseline is complete enough to support credible cost and opportunity analysis.
questions.answerDesign: Select every category that is included in the reported spend figure. Use the reconciliation option when the boundary is unclear.
questions.evidenceImplication: Tests baseline completeness

options.label: Infrastructure and data centres
Public / private cloud
SaaS subscriptions
Software licences
Application development and support
Network and connectivity
Data platforms and analytics
Cybersecurity
Internal technology workforce
External services and systems integrators
Workplace / end-user computing
Other material technology spend
I cannot confidently reconcile what is included

questions.answerGuidance: Answer based on what is actually included in the number you gave in CORE-04, not what should ideally be included.

questions.prompt: How confident are you that the technology-spend baseline is complete enough to support executive decisions, including material business-led technology spend?
questions.intent: Separate confidence in the data baseline from the maturity of the cost-management process.
questions.answerDesign: Rate confidence, not performance. Five cumulative stars represent increasing confidence in completeness and reconciliation.
questions.evidenceImplication: Requests validation of excluded spend

labels: Significant gaps are likely
Several material gaps remain
Most major spend is visible, but gaps remain
Broadly complete, with limited gaps
Comprehensive and reconciled

questions.answerGuidance: Think about omissions, indirect spend, business-led technology and inconsistent cost ownership.

questions.prompt: Looking ahead 12–24 months, which three technology outcomes should receive the strongest protection when trade-offs are made?
questions.intent: Capture the CIO’s explicit investment priorities and the outcomes that should be protected when cost and value trade-offs are made.
questions.answerDesign: Select exactly three outcomes, then rank those three from highest to lowest priority.
questions.evidenceImplication: Links investment priorities to roadmap

options.label: Reduce recurring run cost while protecting service levels
Increase measurable business value from technology
Modernize aging platforms and infrastructure
Accelerate strategic and digital transformation
Increase resilience, continuity and recoverability
Strengthen cybersecurity and reduce technology risk
Scale AI / GenAI into priority business use cases
Reduce technology complexity and technical debt
Improve employee productivity through better technology
Increase the ability to redirect technology as priorities change

questions.answerGuidance: Rank outcomes that should survive funding pressure—not activities that are simply important today.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the cost pressure leadership expects technology to manage over the next 12 months?
questions.intent: Distinguish routine efficiency expectations from a formal, urgent or investment-constraining cost mandate.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the single statement that best reflects the current executive mandate.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: High cost pressure activates cost-reduction deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Sets urgency

options.label: Cost is monitored, but there is no material executive pressure to reduce it.
Efficiency expectations are increasing and leaders want visible improvement.
Technology cost reduction is an explicit executive priority for the next 12 months.
Significant savings are expected within the next 12 months and difficult trade-offs are already underway.
Cost pressure is already constraining investment in strategic technology priorities.

questions.answerGuidance: Select the situation leadership is actually managing, rather than the level of cost pressure you think it should have.

questions.prompt: Before seeing any assessment findings, where would you expect the largest opportunities to improve technology value? Select up to five areas, then rank the three you would investigate first.
questions.intent: Capture the CIO’s starting hypothesis before the diagnostic engine presents its own findings, enabling useful comparison between perception and evidence.
questions.answerDesign: Select up to five areas that appear promising; rank the three you would investigate first.
questions.evidenceImplication: Creates hypothesis list

options.label: Retire or consolidate low-value, duplicate or overlapping technology
Improve cloud consumption, architecture and platform economics
Improve technology workforce productivity and capacity utilization
Improve supplier commercials, scope and sourcing economics
Improve economics and outcomes from data and AI investments
Reduce complexity, duplication and technical debt
Automate manual technology operations and service activities
Improve product engineering and delivery economics
Improve measurement and realization of technology benefits
Align technology spend more tightly to business priorities

questions.answerGuidance: This is your hypothesis—not the assessment conclusion. Choose areas where you would expect better value, lower waste or stronger outcomes.
questions.hypothesisComparison: Compare selected/ranked areas with engine-identified opportunity areas in executive report; no score impact.

questions.prompt: Which change in the way technology is funded would most improve the value you can get from the current budget?
questions.intent: Identify the structural funding change that would most improve transparency, outcome accountability, flexibility or portfolio discipline.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the one funding-model change that would have the greatest practical effect.
questions.evidenceImplication: May require governance evidence

options.label: Make spend, allocations and unit costs more transparent so leaders can challenge trade-offs.
Tie funding more directly to measurable business outcomes and benefits.
Make a larger share of funding easier to redirect as priorities change.
Move suitable funding from projects toward products / services with ongoing accountability.
Use enterprise portfolio governance to stop lower-value demand and reallocate funds.
Clarify which funding decisions belong with central IT, business or product teams.
The current funding model is broadly fit for purpose.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose the change that would most improve decision quality or redirectability of existing spend.

questions.prompt: When business priorities change materially, which statement best describes how quickly you can redirect technology funding and capacity?
questions.intent: Assess strategic agility and identify structural commitments that make technology funding and capacity difficult to redirect.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement that best describes the normal operating reality—not an exceptional case.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Low agility activates funding deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Requires commitment/contract evidence

options.label: We can redirect discretionary funding and capacity within weeks.
We can redirect a meaningful portion within one quarter through normal governance.
Redirection requires significant reprioritization and usually spans multiple quarters.
Most funding or capacity is tied up in existing contracts, platforms or run commitments.
Redirecting funding or capacity is currently difficult and creates major disruption.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider funding commitments, contracts, platform run costs, delivery capacity and governance lead time.

questions.prompt: When you need to explain where technology money goes, how far can you take that analysis today?
questions.intent: Assess whether leaders can move from a total technology spend figure to a reliable view of categories, owners, services and business use.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement that best reflects the level of spend transparency available today.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate enterprise spend baseline, material business-led spend and reconciliation logic.

options.label: We can reconcile enterprise technology spend to major categories, owners, services/products and material business-led spend.
We have an enterprise view, but some material business-led, indirect or shared spend remains outside it.
We can see major spend categories, but allocation to services, products or business units is inconsistent.
We mainly see spend by vendors, towers, departments or projects and struggle to build an enterprise picture.
We do not have a reliable enterprise technology spend baseline.

scoring.note: Direct maturity signal for Spend Transparency.

questions.answerGuidance: Answer from what leaders can actually see and reconcile today — not what finance, IT or procurement intends to build.
questions.opportunityImplication: Strengthen the enterprise technology spend baseline before sizing optimization opportunities.
questions.confidenceImpact: Baseline completeness materially affects confidence in downstream opportunity sizing.

questions.prompt: At what level can technology cost be routinely understood and challenged today?
questions.intent: Assess whether cost is traceable to a useful management object rather than only accounting or procurement categories.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the description closest to how cost is managed in the majority of the estate.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate allocation rules, service catalog/unit-cost models, cost-centre mappings and material exceptions.

options.label: By service/product, with clear owners, consumers and major cost drivers or unit economics.
By business unit or business-facing product, with useful allocation but limited unit-cost detail.
By technology tower/platform, with limited allocation to consumers or services.
Primarily through vendors, contracts or procurement categories rather than the services they support.
Primarily through projects/programs, with weak visibility into ongoing service economics.
Primarily through general-ledger categories or cost centres.
Several models coexist, but practice varies materially across the estate.

scoring.note: Score reflects decision usefulness of cost attribution, not preference for a specific accounting model.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on the level leaders can routinely use to understand cost drivers and make decisions.
questions.opportunityImplication: Identify cost pools where improved allocation would expose leakage or enable business/value trade-offs.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low allocation traceability reduces confidence in category-level opportunity sizing.

questions.prompt: Which material technology cost areas are hardest to attribute to a clear owner, service/product or cost driver?
questions.intent: Identify where allocation and ownership gaps are concentrated so later diagnostics can focus on material leakage rather than asking the same questions everywhere.
questions.answerDesign: Select all material problem areas. Select 'None material' only when allocation is broadly workable.
questions.evidenceImplication: Request category-specific allocation evidence only for selected areas.

options.label: Cloud consumption / shared cloud platforms
Shared infrastructure / data-centre platforms
SaaS subscriptions and shared licences
Enterprise software and licensing
Network and connectivity
Data platforms, storage and analytics
Cybersecurity and security platforms
Internal technology workforce
External services / systems integrators / managed services
Applications and product teams
Other material shared technology cost
None material — attribution is broadly workable

scoring.note: Do not score by number of selections. Use selected categories to activate evidence and leakage diagnostics.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about material spend that leaders cannot explain beyond a shared pool, vendor, tower or departmental budget.
questions.opportunityImplication: Use selected categories to target visibility and allocation leakage assessment.
questions.confidenceImpact: Selected gaps lower confidence for opportunity sizing in the affected cost pools.

questions.prompt: How quickly can executives obtain a consolidated technology cost view that is current enough to act on?
questions.intent: Assess whether cost intelligence arrives with a cadence and freshness that supports intervention rather than retrospective reporting.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the normal operating cadence and usability level.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate reporting cadence, data freshness, reconciliations and examples of decisions made from the cost view.

options.label: Self-service/current dashboards are available when leadership needs them, with sufficiently fresh data.
A monthly view is available and includes enough context to challenge major movements.
A quarterly view is available and is mainly used for management or budget reviews.
The consolidated view is mainly available twice a year or during planning cycles.
The view is primarily annual or part of the formal budget process.
A consolidated view is assembled mainly when a specific issue, renewal or escalation occurs.
There is no dependable consolidated executive technology cost view.

scoring.note: Cadence is one contributor to governance maturity; data quality still drives confidence separately.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose how the information actually works for leadership today, including whether it is current enough to challenge significant movements.
questions.opportunityImplication: Improve cost intelligence cadence where slow or ad hoc reporting delays intervention.
questions.confidenceImpact: Poor cadence can limit evidence timeliness even when a baseline exists.

questions.prompt: Is material technology spend initiated, owned or controlled outside the central technology organization?
questions.intent: Identify business-led or decentralized technology spend that may create visibility, duplication or governance gaps.
questions.answerDesign: Answer whether material spend exists outside central technology; use unsure where the boundary cannot be confidently established.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate decentralized procurement, finance records, SaaS inventories and business-owned technology.

options.label: Yes — material business-led or decentralized technology spend exists.
No — material technology spend is centrally governed or reconciled.
We cannot confidently determine the amount outside central technology.

scoring.note: This is a scope/governance trigger, not a direct maturity score.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider SaaS, data/AI, local applications, departmental platforms, engineering tools and externally procured technology that may not sit in the central IT budget.
questions.opportunityImplication: Assess shadow-tech duplication, commercial leakage and governance gaps where material spend sits outside central IT.
questions.confidenceImpact: Unknown decentralized spend materially reduces confidence in the enterprise baseline.

questions.prompt: Approximately what percentage of technology spend can be traced to a clear owner, service/product and primary cost driver?
questions.intent: Quantify attribution coverage directly without requiring an exact enterprise allocation calculation.
questions.answerDesign: Use a best defensible percentage estimate; exact precision is not required.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate allocation coverage for the largest spend pools and material exceptions.
questions.answerGuidance: Estimate the share of spend where leadership can identify who owns it, what service/product it supports and the main driver of cost. Use Unknown when a percentage would be misleading.
questions.opportunityImplication: Focus deeper diagnostic effort where spend remains unattributed or pooled.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low traceability lowers confidence in category-level economic conclusions.

questions.prompt: When technology spend no longer delivers the expected value, how strong are the decision rights to challenge, reduce or stop it?
questions.intent: Assess whether enterprise governance has practical authority to act on underperforming spend.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement closest to what can actually happen, not merely what policy allows.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate governance charter, decision rights, examples of challenged investments and stop/reduce decisions.

options.label: Cross-enterprise portfolio governance can challenge, reduce or stop spend across business and technology.
Technology leadership can challenge or stop discretionary technology spend within a defined mandate.
Finance/procurement can challenge defined categories, contracts or budgets, but not always the underlying demand.
Budget or service owners can challenge spend within their own area, with limited enterprise intervention.
There is no consistent decision right; exceptions, commitments or business dependencies usually prevail.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about whether leaders can challenge funding, reduce scope, stop renewals or redirect capacity when evidence shows value is weak.
questions.opportunityImplication: Establish a repeatable challenge mechanism for low-value or underperforming spend.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak challenge evidence increases uncertainty around the practicality of identified rationalization opportunities.

questions.prompt: For a material technology investment, which evidence is routinely required before funding is approved?
questions.intent: Assess whether investment decisions are supported by sufficient economic, outcome, risk and operating evidence before money is committed.
questions.answerDesign: Select the evidence that is routinely required in the normal approval process. Do not select items required only for exceptional investments.
questions.evidenceImplication: Request a sample of recent investment approvals and compare stated requirements with actual evidence used.

options.label: Clear strategic/business rationale and expected contribution
Business case with alternatives and investment rationale
Total cost of ownership / lifecycle cost
Quantified expected benefits with accountable owners
Risk, security, resilience or regulatory impact
Architecture, dependency and technology impact
People, operating model and capacity impact
Commercial options, sourcing and contractual analysis
Defined outcome metrics, baseline and post-delivery measurement plan
No consistent evidence set is required across material investments

scoring.note: Do not score by simple option count; evaluate combinations and required evidence patterns in the deterministic engine.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose what approval bodies consistently see, not what a strong business case would ideally contain.
questions.opportunityImplication: Strengthen investment discipline where economic or benefit evidence is missing before funding.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak pre-investment evidence reduces confidence in portfolio-level value conclusions.

questions.prompt: After a major technology investment goes live, what normally happens to the business outcomes that were expected?
questions.intent: Assess whether benefits are owned, measured and acted upon after implementation.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the operating reality for the majority of material investments.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate benefit registers, post-implementation reviews, KPI baselines/targets and examples of corrective action.

options.label: Benefits have accountable owners, baselines, targets, review dates and action when outcomes miss.
Benefits are tracked for the largest investments, but not consistently across the portfolio.
Benefits are estimated in the business case but are rarely revisited after delivery.
We mainly track delivery, adoption or usage metrics rather than business outcomes.
There is no systematic process for checking whether expected benefits were achieved.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on what happens after delivery — including whether misses trigger corrective action, scope changes or future funding decisions.
questions.opportunityImplication: Improve benefits realization and use outcome evidence to redirect future technology investment.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak benefit measurement reduces confidence in Value IQ and in opportunities framed as value realization.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches how most technology investment and run spend is funded today?
questions.intent: Understand the structural funding model and the constraints it creates for cost ownership, value management and redirection.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the dominant model; mixed models are acceptable where the estate genuinely operates differently by domain.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate budget structures, funding commitments, reallocation rules, run/change split and examples of in-year funding movement.

options.label: Funding is primarily tied to products/services and measurable business outcomes.
Funding is primarily tied to technology services and their consumption or service economics.
Funding is primarily organized around projects and programs, with limited ongoing product/service ownership.
Funding is primarily assigned to technology towers or platforms.
Most funding is locked into annual budgets with limited reallocation during the year.
Different funding models coexist and the enterprise has no clearly dominant model.

scoring.note: Model type is not judged in isolation; score should be reconciled with actual redirectability and governance evidence.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider how funding is actually committed and governed across run, change, products/services and major programs.
questions.opportunityImplication: Identify structural funding constraints that prevent investment redirection or continuation of low-value spend.
questions.confidenceImpact: Funding rigidity is a practical constraint that should moderate actionable opportunity, not erase economic opportunity.

questions.prompt: When a technology product, service or investment underperforms, what normally happens next?
questions.intent: Assess whether portfolio governance creates a repeatable intervention path before weak performance becomes entrenched spend.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes normal practice.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate portfolio review cadence, intervention thresholds and examples where funding/scope/ownership changed after performance review.

options.label: Performance/value thresholds trigger formal review and intervention, including reduce, redirect or stop decisions.
Formal portfolio reviews occur at least annually and can result in funding or scope changes.
Challenge mainly occurs during budget, planning or renewal cycles.
Intervention usually starts only after costs, delivery or business dissatisfaction become problematic.
Underperforming spend is rarely challenged or materially changed.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about the trigger for intervention and whether leaders can change funding, scope, ownership or continuation.
questions.opportunityImplication: Create portfolio challenge and stop/reduce mechanisms to prevent low-value spend from persisting.
questions.confidenceImpact: Weak intervention history lowers confidence that economically attractive rationalization is practically executable.

questions.prompt: Which technology environments are materially used today and should be included in the cost and value analysis?
questions.intent: Activate only the environment-specific diagnostics that are relevant to the enterprise.
questions.answerDesign: Select every environment that is materially used. Choose 'None of these are material' only when none is a meaningful part of the technology estate.
questions.evidenceImplication: Use architecture/inventory evidence to confirm the material environment footprint.
questions.findingImplication: Determines which cloud, virtualization, infrastructure and service-economics findings can be considered.

options.label: Public cloud platforms and services
Private cloud or hosted private infrastructure
VMware or other virtualization platforms
Traditional on-premises infrastructure and data centres
SaaS applications and subscriptions
Colocation or third-party data-centre facilities
Managed infrastructure or technology services
None of these are material

scoring.note: Scope trigger only; never score by number of environments selected.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about environments that materially drive spend, contracts, operations or technology decisions—not every environment that exists somewhere in the business.
questions.opportunityImplication: Sets the addressable spend scope; does not itself create an opportunity.
questions.confidenceImpact: Scope completeness; selected environments become the minimum evidence boundary.

questions.prompt: When cloud spend changes materially, what normally happens to explain and act on the change?
questions.intent: Assess whether cloud economics are actively managed at workload and consumption level rather than only through budget reporting.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement that best matches normal operating practice when cloud spend moves materially.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Deepens cloud economics diagnostic when PUBLIC_CLOUD is selected
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with cloud cost dashboards, allocation data, optimization actions and ownership records.
questions.findingImplication: May indicate consumption leakage when material spend movements cannot be explained or acted upon quickly.

options.label: A material change is automatically surfaced to an accountable owner, investigated to workload level and followed by corrective action.
FinOps or cloud owners review material changes regularly and take action within the normal reporting cycle.
Changes are visible, but investigation and action depend on the individual team or issue.
Spend is mostly reviewed through budget reports; root-cause analysis is usually reactive.
Cloud spend can be seen, but we cannot consistently explain changes at workload or service level.
We do not have dependable visibility into material cloud consumption changes.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about what really happens after a material increase or decrease: who investigates it, how quickly, and whether corrective action follows.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate cloud consumption optimization and rightsizing opportunity logic.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; validate against cloud cost and optimization evidence.

questions.prompt: Which cloud cost-management practices are actually used in day-to-day technology decisions?
questions.intent: Identify cloud economics controls and practices that are operational—not merely planned or available in tooling.
questions.answerDesign: Select practices that are genuinely used to make decisions today. Do not select capabilities that exist only as policy, tooling features or future plans.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate selected practices with operating reports, policy configurations, optimization tickets and owner accountability.
questions.findingImplication: Patterns such as visibility without action or missing allocation/automation may indicate consumption or governance leakage.

options.label: Cloud spend is allocated to business, product, service or accountable owner.
Budgets, alerts or anomaly detection trigger action—not just notification.
Rightsizing and workload optimization recommendations are routinely acted upon.
Reservations, Savings Plans or committed-use discounts are actively sized and reviewed.
Cloud forecasts are used in budgeting, product planning or investment decisions.
Cloud cost is linked to useful business/product demand or unit economics where appropriate.
Policies or guardrails prevent avoidable consumption before it occurs.
Automated remediation handles recurring waste or non-compliant consumption.
None of these practices are consistently used in day-to-day decisions.

scoring.note: Do not score by selection count; evaluate combinations and evidence in the intelligence engine.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose what teams actually use when they allocate, forecast, optimize or approve cloud consumption.
questions.opportunityImplication: Activates specific cloud diagnostics rather than scoring the number of practices selected.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low-to-medium; presence of a practice does not prove effectiveness.

questions.prompt: How confidently can you match major SaaS subscriptions to active usage and business need before renewal?
questions.intent: Assess whether SaaS economics are driven by actual usage and business need rather than purchased seat counts alone.
questions.answerDesign: Rate the level of confidence leadership has in using usage and business-need evidence before major SaaS renewals.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Deepens SaaS economics diagnostic when SAAS is selected
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate major subscriptions using user counts, utilization telemetry, business-owner confirmation and renewal decisions.
questions.findingImplication: Low confidence may indicate unused or poorly aligned SaaS spend.

options.label: Usage is continuously measured and licences are adjusted as demand changes.
Utilization is reviewed before major renewals and meaningful reductions are made.
Some major products have utilization data, but coverage is inconsistent.
We mainly manage licence counts and contracts rather than actual usage.
Actual utilization is largely unknown.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider active users, feature utilization, business-owner validation, overlapping products and whether renewal quantities change based on evidence.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate SaaS licence right-sizing and renewal challenge analysis.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; test against usage and renewal evidence.

labels.1: Usage and business need are largely unknown
labels.2: We know basic seat counts, but usage evidence is limited
labels.3: Major products have useful usage data, but reviews are inconsistent
labels.4: Major renewals are usually challenged using usage and business-owner evidence
labels.5: Usage and business need routinely drive subscription quantities and renewal decisions

questions.prompt: When two SaaS products provide overlapping capability, what normally happens?
questions.intent: Assess whether overlapping SaaS capability is identified and converted into portfolio decisions.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes what happens when meaningful SaaS overlap is identified.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using application inventory, capability maps, contracts and consolidation decisions.
questions.findingImplication: Weak challenge of overlapping capability can indicate SaaS or portfolio leakage.

options.label: Enterprise portfolio governance actively consolidates overlapping products and tracks the value released.
Major overlaps are reviewed by the relevant business and technology owners and consolidation decisions are made when justified.
Overlap is documented, but decisions are inconsistent or depend on local owners.
Overlap is mainly challenged when a renewal or significant cost event is approaching.
There is no consistent process to identify and rationalize overlapping SaaS capability.
We do not have enough visibility to identify meaningful SaaS overlap reliably.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on whether overlap leads to consolidation, ownership decisions and measurable value release—or simply gets documented.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate duplicate-SaaS consolidation opportunity sizing.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; validate material overlap and actual decisions.

questions.prompt: When cloud or SaaS demand changes, how much practical flexibility do you have to change major commercial commitments?
questions.intent: Separate commercial economics from practical feasibility by identifying contractual lock-in affecting optimization.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the statement that best reflects what the organization can realistically change—not what contracts theoretically permit.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Deepens commercial economics diagnostic when PUBLIC_CLOUD or SAAS is selected
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate major commitments using contracts, renewal calendars, commitment utilization and change/termination clauses.
questions.findingImplication: Material lock-in can create commercial leakage and constrain otherwise attractive optimization actions.

options.label: Commitments can be actively re-sized, reallocated or changed as demand changes, with limited commercial friction.
Most commitments are reviewed routinely and material changes can usually be negotiated or rebalanced.
Some commitments are flexible, but material changes often wait for defined commercial windows.
Major commitments materially limit near-term flexibility; renewal or contract events drive most change.
Contractual lock-in materially constrains optimization decisions and creates significant execution friction.
The organization does not have dependable visibility into the terms or flexibility of major commitments.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider committed spend, minimums, termination rights, renewal dates, price protections, portability and the ability to reduce or reallocate commitments without major disruption.
questions.opportunityImplication: Report economic opportunity separately from practical opportunity where contractual lock-in reduces near-term actionability.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium until major commitments and contract terms are evidenced.

questions.prompt: Which software and licensing areas warrant the strongest economic or compliance review?
questions.intent: Identify licensing domains most likely to contain cost, compliance or renewal exposure.
questions.answerDesign: Select areas where spend, usage uncertainty, contract exposure, audit risk or renewal activity makes deeper review worthwhile.
questions.evidenceImplication: Use entitlement records, deployment/usage evidence, contracts, audit history and renewal calendars.
questions.findingImplication: Selected categories become targeted licensing economics hotspots.

options.label: Database platforms and database licensing
Virtualization platforms, including VMware
ERP and other major enterprise applications
Operating systems and infrastructure software
Middleware, integration and data-platform licensing
Security and compliance software
Developer, engineering and specialist tools
Productivity, collaboration and end-user software
Other material software/licensing exposure
No material licensing area currently stands out

scoring.note: Do not score by count; use selected areas to activate targeted diagnostics.

questions.answerGuidance: Select material areas—not every type of software in the estate. Several are appropriate when exposure is broad.
questions.opportunityImplication: Activates rightsizing, consolidation, commercial and compliance opportunity diagnostics.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low; hotspot signal requiring evidence.

questions.prompt: When software deployment or usage changes, how reliably are licence entitlements reconciled before the next commercial event?
questions.intent: Assess whether purchased entitlement, actual deployment and actual usage are connected well enough to make licensing decisions.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern closest to normal practice for major software publishers.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate against entitlement repositories, deployment discovery, utilization data and publisher contracts.
questions.findingImplication: Weak reconciliation can create both unused-license cost and compliance/true-up exposure.

options.label: Entitlement, deployment and usage are reconciled routinely enough to drive licence changes as conditions change.
Major software estates are reconciled periodically and normally inform renewal or deployment decisions.
Reconciliation exists for selected publishers or products, but coverage is inconsistent.
Reconciliation is mainly performed before renewals, audits or major changes.
We manage purchased entitlements more reliably than actual deployment or usage.
We cannot reliably establish the current licence position for material software.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about what happens before renewals, audits, migrations or major deployment changes—not only whether an inventory tool exists.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate licence optimization, contract preparation and audit-risk diagnostics.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; actual entitlement/usage reconciliation evidence is required for financial sizing.

questions.prompt: Which material software, cloud or SaaS commercial events could affect technology decisions in the next 12–24 months?
questions.intent: Identify time-bound commercial events that could create an optimization, renegotiation, migration or rationalization window.
questions.answerDesign: Select every event material enough to influence technology or investment decisions. Exact dates and values are captured during evidence validation.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate selected events using contract/renewal calendars, commercial terms, product roadmaps and owner evidence.
questions.findingImplication: Creates time-sensitive commercial signals without assuming every event creates savings.

options.label: Major cloud commitment, minimum-spend or pricing event
Major SaaS or software renewal
Publisher audit, licence true-up or compliance event
Known or expected vendor price increase / commercial reset
Contract expiry or termination window that creates a real change option
End-of-support, product retirement or forced migration event
Savings Plan, reservation or committed-use term expiry
Planned enterprise consolidation, sourcing event or platform standardization
No material event is currently visible
The commercial-event calendar is not sufficiently visible to know

scoring.note: Event presence is a timing signal, not a maturity score.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider the next 12–24 months, including events already known to procurement, finance, IT or business owners.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can bring forward opportunities when a renewal, expiry, audit or migration window makes change more practical.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low until event dates, spend and terms are evidenced.

questions.prompt: Which infrastructure areas show the clearest potential for excess capacity, underutilization or avoidable footprint?
questions.intent: Identify infrastructure cost-leakage hotspots for targeted utilization and footprint analysis.
questions.answerDesign: Select areas where leadership sees credible concern based on utilization, capacity, footprint, refresh or operating-cost patterns.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using utilization telemetry, capacity plans, asset inventories, facility costs and refresh roadmaps.
questions.findingImplication: Selected areas identify where excess capacity or avoidable footprint should be tested.

options.label: Compute / server capacity
Storage capacity and tiering
Network and connectivity capacity
Data-centre footprint, power or facility capacity
Backup and disaster-recovery capacity
Virtualization clusters and host utilization
End-user computing / workplace estate
Specialist infrastructure or appliances
No material infrastructure capacity concern currently stands out

scoring.note: Do not score by selection count.

questions.answerGuidance: Choose material hotspots, not every infrastructure category. Use 'None' only when there is no clear concern today.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate right-sizing, consolidation, hosting and lifecycle opportunity analysis.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low-to-medium; perceived hotspots require utilization evidence.

questions.prompt: When infrastructure capacity is planned or refreshed, what normally drives the decision?
questions.intent: Assess whether infrastructure capacity is sized from demand and utilization evidence rather than defaulting to lifecycle refresh or conservative headroom.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes normal infrastructure planning and refresh decisions.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with capacity forecasts, utilization reports, refresh approvals and consolidation decisions.
questions.findingImplication: Lifecycle- or risk-led provisioning without demand evidence may indicate excess-footprint leakage.

options.label: Demand forecasts, utilization and service requirements are combined to size, consolidate or retire capacity before major purchases.
Utilization and demand are reviewed regularly and materially influence capacity and refresh decisions.
Capacity is reviewed during planning or refresh, but actual utilization is not always decisive.
Refresh and lifecycle standards usually drive capacity; conservative headroom is kept to protect availability.
Capacity is deliberately maintained above expected demand because service risk is difficult to quantify.
Utilization and demand are not reliable enough to determine whether the current footprint is appropriately sized.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about what evidence actually determines how much capacity is bought, retained or retired.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate right-sizing, consolidation and lifecycle optimization diagnostics.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; capacity evidence should be available for material platforms.

questions.prompt: Approximately what share of recurring technology operations effort still involves manual work that could reasonably be simplified, automated or self-served?
questions.intent: Estimate operational productivity leakage without requiring a detailed activity study in the executive scan.
questions.answerDesign: Estimate the percentage of recurring operations effort where the work is repetitive and a credible simplification, automation or self-service path exists.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate high estimates using process inventories, ticket volumes, runbooks, service metrics and automation candidates.
questions.findingImplication: A high addressable manual-work share may indicate operations productivity leakage.

scoring.note: Higher addressable manual work indicates greater leakage and therefore lowers maturity score.

control.rightLabel: 100% — most recurring work is potentially addressable

questions.answerGuidance: Estimate current addressable manual work—not all manual work. Do not assume every manual activity should be automated or that automation is free.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can create productivity opportunity ranges, subject to evidence and change-capacity constraints.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; directional estimate until process/time evidence is available.

questions.prompt: How reliably can the organization align technology workforce capacity and skills to the demand it actually needs to deliver?
questions.intent: Assess workforce economics by testing whether staffing, skills and demand are actively matched rather than managed through reactive escalation.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the operating state that best describes normal enterprise practice today.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Activates workforce productivity and sourcing deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using workforce inventory, demand/capacity data, skills matrices, contractor mix, utilization and delivery throughput.
questions.findingImplication: Material mismatch or weak measurement may indicate workforce productivity/cost leakage.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate workforce capacity, skills and sourcing optimization; quantify only after evidence validation.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; executive perception should be validated with workforce and demand evidence.

options.label: Capacity and critical skills are measured against demand and routinely rebalanced as priorities change.
The workforce is generally aligned, with a few hotspots handled through normal management.
Some teams are overloaded while others have spare capacity, underused skills or persistent bottlenecks.
Material skill or capacity mismatches are affecting delivery, cost or the ability to meet demand.
Demand, capacity and skills are not measured consistently enough to judge the fit.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about current operating reality across employees, contractors, managed services and specialist skills—not the target operating model.

questions.prompt: Approximately what share of technology workforce capacity is supplied through external parties such as managed services, contractors, system integrators or specialist providers?
questions.intent: Establish external workforce exposure that may affect unit economics, flexibility, sourcing and practical change capacity.
questions.answerDesign: Select the broad band that best reflects total technology delivery and operations capacity supplied externally.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: External workforce share above 25% activates sourcing and commercial deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using workforce inventory, supplier statements of work, managed-service contracts, contractor counts and spend.
questions.findingImplication: High external dependency can be a diagnostic signal for sourcing economics or flexibility constraints; it is not inherently inefficient.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate sourcing, rate-card, contract, insource/outsource and capacity-flexibility analysis.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; percentage estimate should be evidenced before opportunity sizing.

options.label: Below 10%
More than 75%
Not known / prefer not to disclose

scoring.note: Context/exposure signal; do not infer that a higher external share is inherently better or worse.

questions.answerGuidance: Use total technology workforce capacity, not only permanent employees. Include managed services and material contractor/SI capacity where it is operationally equivalent to internal capacity.

questions.prompt: How consistently does vendor governance use cost, consumption, outcomes and commercial levers—not only service-level performance?
questions.intent: Assess whether vendor management actively protects economic value throughout the contract lifecycle.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes how material strategic technology suppliers are normally governed.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with QBR packs, scorecards, consumption data, rate cards, benchmark clauses, savings actions and renewal plans.
questions.findingImplication: Service-level-only governance or renewal-time intervention may indicate commercial leakage.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate supplier commercial optimization and contract/consumption diagnostics.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; commercial opportunity requires contract and spend evidence.

options.label: Strategic suppliers are governed against outcomes, consumption, total cost, performance and commercial value throughout the lifecycle.
Regular service and commercial reviews are held, with actions and value opportunities tracked.
Governance is active, but attention is primarily on SLA and operational performance.
Commercial challenge becomes a major focus mainly when renewal or rebid approaches.
Ongoing commercial and value governance is limited after the contract is signed.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on material technology suppliers and whether economics are actively managed after contracting, not just whether supplier performance meetings occur.

questions.prompt: If you were to investigate the technology commercial portfolio first, which supplier categories would you examine for the greatest potential value? Rank up to three.
questions.intent: Capture the CIO's vendor opportunity hypothesis before the assessment engine identifies evidence-led opportunities.
questions.answerDesign: Rank the three supplier categories you would investigate first.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Activates targeted vendor commercial deep dives for selected categories
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate the hypothesis against supplier spend, concentration, contract terms, rate cards, consumption and renewal calendar.
questions.findingImplication: Signals where leadership expects commercial opportunity; it is not itself a finding.
questions.opportunityImplication: Provides a targeted starting point for evidence-led commercial validation.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low until spend and contract evidence validates the hypothesis.

options.label: Cloud providers and hyperscalers
Enterprise software and licensing publishers
System integrators and application delivery partners
Managed infrastructure, cloud or operations services
Telecom, network and connectivity providers
Infrastructure, hardware and hosting suppliers
Specialist technology or niche service providers

scoring.note: Do not score by ranking position; compare leadership hypothesis with evidence-led findings.

questions.answerGuidance: Rank where you suspect the strongest commercial or sourcing opportunity exists, not the categories with the largest spend by default.

questions.prompt: Which application-portfolio conditions are currently contributing to avoidable cost, complexity or management effort?
questions.intent: Identify application cost and complexity hotspots that should drive targeted rationalization analysis.
questions.answerDesign: Select the conditions that are materially present in the current application estate.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Selected hotspot activates application rationalization deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using application inventory, usage, support cost, business owner, lifecycle, dependency and contract data.
questions.findingImplication: Selected hotspots can support an application economics finding after evidence validation.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate rationalization, consolidation, lifecycle and retirement opportunity analysis.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low; hotspot perception requires portfolio evidence.

options.label: Multiple applications provide overlapping or duplicate capabilities.
Legacy applications require disproportionate support or specialist skills.
Applications have low or declining usage relative to their cost.
Applications generate high support, incident or maintenance effort.
Complex integrations or point-to-point interfaces add material cost or effort.
Platforms or applications are approaching end-of-life or unsupported technology.
Heavy customization increases upgrade, testing or support cost.
Business ownership, value or decision rights are unclear.
Other material application cost/complexity issue
None of these conditions are materially present

scoring.note: Do not score by selection count; use selected conditions to activate diagnostics and evidence requests.

questions.answerGuidance: Select only conditions that are material enough to influence cost, complexity or portfolio decisions. Selecting many options does not imply better or worse maturity.

questions.prompt: How much does technology complexity or technical debt contribute to current technology operating cost?
questions.intent: Assess whether architecture complexity and accumulated debt are active economic drivers rather than purely technical concerns.
questions.answerDesign: Rate the current economic impact of complexity and technical debt.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: High impact activates architecture / technical debt deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with architecture assessments, dependency maps, incident/problem records, run-cost analysis, upgrade effort and technical-debt registers.
questions.findingImplication: Higher economic impact can support an architecture/technical-debt cost leakage finding.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate modernization, simplification and technical-debt reduction opportunity analysis.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; perceived impact should be linked to observable cost or effort evidence.

labels: 1 — Little or no material cost impact
2 — Some cost and effort, but limited
3 — Meaningful contributor in several areas
4 — Major contributor to run cost or delivery effort
5 — One of the most significant structural cost drivers

questions.answerGuidance: Consider extra infrastructure, integration, support, testing, specialist skills, upgrade effort and delivery friction caused by complexity or debt.

questions.prompt: How systematically does the organization decide which applications to retain, modernize, consolidate or retire?
questions.intent: Assess whether application portfolio decisions are driven by value, cost and strategic fit rather than isolated project events.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes normal portfolio management practice.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with portfolio review outputs, application disposition decisions, owner sign-off, cost/usage data and retirement roadmaps.
questions.findingImplication: Inconsistent or event-driven rationalization may indicate avoidable portfolio cost.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate rationalization, consolidation, retirement and modernization sequencing.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; actual portfolio decisions should be evidenced.

options.label: Applications are routinely assessed against business value, cost, risk, usage and strategic fit, with clear disposition decisions.
Formal rationalization reviews occur periodically and usually lead to action.
Rationalization mainly happens during transformation, migration, renewal or major architecture events.
Duplication is understood, but business dependencies or ownership make decisions difficult.
There is no consistent enterprise process for deciding what to retain, consolidate or retire.

questions.answerGuidance: Focus on actual portfolio decisions and governance. A policy or inventory alone does not count as systematic rationalization.

questions.prompt: When application retirement or consolidation is considered, which constraints most often make the change difficult or slow?
questions.intent: Formalize practical feasibility by capturing business, regulatory, contractual and technology constraints that can limit otherwise attractive economic opportunities.
questions.answerDesign: Select every material constraint that commonly affects application rationalization decisions.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Selected constraints activate feasibility and sequencing validation
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate selected constraints with dependency maps, criticality classifications, contracts, regulatory controls, data-retention policies, migration plans and change-capacity evidence.
questions.findingImplication: Constraints do not prove that an opportunity is absent; they affect practical actionability and sequencing.
questions.opportunityImplication: Separates economic opportunity from practical opportunity and informs feasibility-adjusted sizing.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; feasibility claims require evidence before practical opportunity is quantified.

options.label: The application is business-critical or difficult to interrupt.
Interfaces, platforms or upstream/downstream dependencies complicate change.
Regulatory, security, resilience or control requirements constrain change.
Vendor contracts, licenses or commitments create lock-in or timing constraints.
Data retention, migration or data-quality requirements make retirement difficult.
Migration effort or transformation dependencies are significant.
Business ownership or decision rights are unclear or contested.
Teams lack sufficient change capacity to execute rationalization alongside other priorities.
User/process change or stakeholder adoption is expected to be difficult.
Other material practical constraint

scoring.note: Do not score by selection count; map selected constraints to practical feasibility assessment.

questions.answerGuidance: Select constraints that materially affect sequencing, timing or feasibility. These constraints should reduce practical actionability, not erase the underlying economic opportunity.

questions.prompt: How would business leaders describe the value they receive from technology relative to the cost they see?
questions.intent: Capture business-facing perception of technology value independently from IT's self-assessment.
questions.answerDesign: Use the observed business stakeholder perspective, not the technology organization's own view.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Low business-value perception activates benefits realization and stakeholder deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with business stakeholder interviews, satisfaction measures, business KPI outcomes and product/service performance evidence.
questions.findingImplication: Low or mixed value perception can indicate a gap between technology cost and perceived business value.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate benefits realization, portfolio alignment and business-value improvement actions.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; perception is directional until triangulated with business evidence.

labels: 1 — Technology cost is widely seen as outweighing the value received
2 — Value is often questioned or inconsistent across major areas
3 — Value is mixed; some areas demonstrate strong value and others do not
4 — Business leaders generally see good value from technology
5 — Technology is consistently viewed as a strong driver of business value

questions.answerGuidance: Think about observed business stakeholder sentiment across major services/products, not one successful or problematic initiative.

questions.prompt: For major technology investments, how consistently does the organization measure whether the expected business outcome was actually achieved?
questions.intent: Assess benefits realization discipline so technology investment can be evaluated on outcomes rather than delivery activity alone.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the description that best matches normal practice for significant technology investments.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Weak benefits discipline activates benefits realization and investment governance deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using business cases, baselines, target KPIs, post-implementation reviews, benefits owners and realized-outcome reporting.
questions.findingImplication: Weak outcome measurement may indicate that transformation or investment value is not consistently realized.
questions.opportunityImplication: Can activate benefits governance, post-implementation review and investment portfolio value improvement.
questions.confidenceImpact: Medium; claimed benefits should be validated against business evidence.

options.label: A quantified baseline and target are defined before approval, then outcome performance is checked after delivery.
Business KPIs are defined and reviewed after implementation for major investments.
We track delivery, adoption, usage or service metrics, but not consistently the business outcome.
Measurement varies by investment and depends heavily on the sponsor or delivery team.
We do not consistently measure whether expected business benefits were achieved.

questions.answerGuidance: Answer for material investments, not only projects where benefits management is especially mature.

questions.prompt: Assume leadership needs to redirect approximately 10% of current technology spend. Which areas would you reduce first, and where would you reinvest the released capacity?

questions.findingImplication: Trade-off profile reveals where leadership is prepared to challenge cost and where it prefers to protect or increase investment.
questions.opportunityImplication: Supports investment-redirection roadmap and comparison with engine-identified opportunity portfolio.
questions.confidenceImpact: Low until financial evidence and strategic priorities validate actionability.

options.label: Reduce legacy infrastructure and technical-debt run cost
Reduce cloud waste and excess consumption
Reduce SaaS/software overlap, unused licenses and subscriptions
Reduce external vendor/service cost through scope or commercial changes
Consolidate or retire low-value/overlapping applications
Reduce manual operations and avoidable process cost
Stop or defer low-outcome discretionary demand
Reinvest in AI/data capabilities with measurable business outcomes
Reinvest in cybersecurity and technology risk reduction
Reinvest in modernization and platform renewal
Reinvest in digital products and customer/employee experience
Reinvest in resilience, continuity and recoverability
Reinvest in automation, platform engineering and productivity
Reinvest in strategic business transformation

scoring.note: Do not score by position. Use as CIO hypothesis/priority signal and compare with assessment-identified opportunities.

questions.answerGuidance: Select the trade-offs you would realistically make under pressure. You do not need to force the selections to mathematically sum to exactly 10%.

questions.prompt: How is public-cloud spend made visible to the teams that consume and influence it?
questions.intent: Assess whether cloud economics are transparent enough for owners to act on consumption and commercial decisions.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the description that best matches how cloud cost accountability works today across material workloads.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using cloud billing exports, tags/account structure, workload ownership and allocation coverage.

options.label: Material cloud spend is attributed to named owners with regular cost visibility and accountability.
Owners receive showback or chargeback information and are expected to manage consumption.
Major workloads can be attributed, but coverage and ownership are inconsistent.
Most spend remains pooled, so owners have limited visibility into the cost they influence.
We cannot reliably connect a meaningful share of cloud spend to owners or workloads.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about whether product, application or business owners can see their relevant cost and are expected to act on it.
questions.confidenceNote: Medium until allocation coverage is evidenced.

questions.prompt: How effectively are non-production cloud environments controlled when they are not needed?
questions.intent: Identify avoidable non-production consumption and the degree to which control is automated.
questions.answerDesign: Select the operating pattern that occurs in normal practice, not only in well-managed teams.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with cloud utilization, scheduling policies, non-production tags, idle-resource reports and exception logs.

options.label: Most material non-production environments follow automated schedules or policy-based scale controls.
Automation covers a meaningful share, with manual exceptions for specific teams or workloads.
Teams manage shutdown and scaling themselves, with inconsistent adherence.
Control is mainly manual and often happens only after spend is noticed.
There is little systematic control over non-production consumption.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider development, test, QA and other non-production environments. Include weekends, nights and inactive periods where relevant.

questions.prompt: How disciplined is the organization in sizing and managing cloud commitments such as reservations or savings plans?
questions.intent: Assess whether contractual cloud discounts are matched to durable demand without creating avoidable commitment risk.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the pattern that best describes how commitments are forecast, purchased, monitored and rebalanced.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with commitment inventory, utilization, coverage, forecast assumptions and renewal history.

options.label: Commitments are based on forecasted baseline demand, monitored continuously and rebalanced as demand changes.
Commitments are centrally monitored and major under- or over-coverage is actively corrected.
Optimization is performed periodically, but provider or team practices vary.
Commitments are mainly revisited around renewals or when utilization problems become visible.
Coverage, utilization and commitment exposure are not sufficiently understood.

questions.prompt: Approximately what share of public-cloud spend cannot currently be traced with confidence to a business owner, product or workload?

questions.answerDesign: Use a broad estimate; actual evidence can be supplied later.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using allocation coverage reports, tags, account hierarchy and workload ownership.
questions.findingImplication: L1 Visibility Leakage / Unallocated cloud spend
questions.answerGuidance: Estimate the share of cloud spend that remains materially unattributed after normal tagging, account and allocation practices.

questions.prompt: How routinely is cloud cost considered alongside performance, resilience and security when architecture decisions are made?

options.label: Cost is a first-class architecture constraint and is evaluated with performance, resilience and security.
Cost is routinely considered for material architecture choices.
Some teams consider cost well, but there is no consistent enterprise expectation.
Cost is usually considered after the architecture is largely established.
Cost is rarely part of architecture decisions.

questions.answerGuidance: Think about architecture reviews, design standards and engineering decisions where a lower-cost option could materially change the outcome.

questions.prompt: How many major SaaS platforms currently overlap materially with other products in the estate?

questions.answerDesign: Use the broad band that best reflects the current portfolio; do not count minor feature overlap.

1–2 major overlapping platforms
3–5 major overlapping platforms
6–10 major overlapping platforms
More than 10 major overlapping platforms
The portfolio is not visible enough to estimate

questions.answerGuidance: Count meaningful capability overlap where two or more major products could plausibly serve substantially the same business need.

questions.prompt: How reliably are unused SaaS licences removed after people leave, change roles or stop using the service?

questions.answerDesign: Select the pattern that best describes actual deprovisioning and inactive-user cleanup.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate using identity events, user activity reports, licence assignments, reclaim logs and renewal true-ups.
questions.findingImplication: L2 Consumption Leakage / Unused SaaS licences

Unused access is normally removed within a defined period through a repeatable process.
Cleanup occurs periodically, but coverage varies materially by platform.
Unused licences are mainly identified when a renewal or audit is approaching.

questions.prompt: Approximately what proportion of SaaS spend is purchased or owned directly by business functions outside central technology governance?

questions.prompt: When evaluating virtualization strategy, how are licensing, infrastructure cost and platform alternatives considered together?

Major renewals include alternative-platform and infrastructure analysis.
Licensing is managed separately from infrastructure and migration economics.
Alternatives are considered mainly when renewal cost becomes a problem.
The organization does not have a reliable integrated view.

questions.prompt: Approximately what proportion of the virtualized estate should be investigated for consolidation, modernization or migration after evidence review?

questions.prompt: How confident are you that data-centre capacity is aligned to realistic current and forecast demand, including resilience requirements?

3 — Demand and capacity are understood for major areas, with some gaps
4 — Capacity is routinely matched to forecast demand with limited excess
5 — Capacity is actively optimized against demand, resilience and forecast growth

questions.answerGuidance: Consider compute, storage, power, cooling and floor space. Include required headroom for resilience and known demand peaks.

questions.prompt: How much of the on-premises estate is approaching a material refresh, support expiry or end-of-life decision?
questions.intent: Identify near-term infrastructure economics and strategic decision windows.
questions.answerDesign: Select the broad proportion of estate entering a material refresh or support decision window over the next 24 months.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with asset inventory, support dates, warranties, vendor roadmaps, refresh plans and workload dependencies.
questions.findingImplication: L3 Commercial Leakage / Refresh decision window

options.label: Below 10%
Above 75%
Lifecycle exposure is not sufficiently visible

questions.prompt: How actively are colocation capacity and contract economics optimized against actual demand?
questions.intent: Assess whether rack, power, space, connectivity and contract commitments are sized and managed economically.
questions.answerDesign: Select the operating pattern that best matches how colocation economics are managed today.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with colocation invoices, rack/power utilization, cross-connect inventory, contract commitments and growth plans.

Major capacity and commercial decisions are reviewed at defined planning points.
Optimization happens periodically, but data or ownership is fragmented.
Capacity is mainly challenged at renewal, expansion or material price change.
Actual utilization and commercial exposure are not sufficiently visible.

questions.prompt: How clearly are managed-service charges connected to the services consumed and the outcomes expected?
questions.intent: Assess whether managed-service economics can be challenged using demand, service levels and outcomes rather than fixed fee alone.
questions.answerDesign: Choose the commercial operating pattern for material managed services.

options.label: Charges are linked to demand, differentiated service levels and measurable outcomes.
Charges are linked reasonably well to service consumption or volumes.
Charges are mainly linked to contracted service levels, with limited demand linkage.
Most charges are fixed, with weak connection to actual consumption or outcomes.
Charges cannot be reliably reconciled to service demand or outcomes.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider volume drivers, service tiers, SLA performance, business outcomes and whether charges change when demand changes.

questions.prompt: Which software categories create the greatest renewal, licensing or commercial exposure over the next 24 months?
questions.intent: Identify where evidence-led licensing and commercial validation should focus first.
questions.answerDesign: Select all material categories; avoid selecting categories that are merely present but not economically significant.
